title: Liver Disease / Abnormal Liver Tests Differential Diagnosis
description: Differential diagnosis for acute and chronic liver disease presenting with abnormal liver chemistries (elevated ALT, AST, alkaline phosphatase, and/or bilirubin) in adults, categorized by hepatocellular, cholestatic, and mixed injury patterns.
source_description: Kwo PY, Cohen SM, Lim JK. ACG Clinical Guideline: Evaluation of Abnormal Liver Chemistries. Am J Gastroenterol 2017;112(1):18-35.

diagnoses.name: Acute Liver Failure
key_features: ALT/AST >15x ULN or >10,000 IU/L
Elevated prothrombin time / INR
Encephalopathy (confusion, asterixis)
Jaundice with coagulopathy
red_flags: Acute hepatitis with elevated PT and/or encephalopathy
recommended_tests: Viral hepatitis panel (HAV IgM, HBsAg, IgM anti-HBc, anti-HCV)

diagnoses.name: Nonalcoholic Fatty Liver Disease (NAFLD/NASH)
key_features: ALT > AST with levels rarely exceeding 300 IU/L
Associated with metabolic syndrome (obesity, diabetes, dyslipidemia, hypertension)
Often asymptomatic or with vague right upper quadrant discomfort
Hepatic steatosis on imaging
red_flags: Advanced fibrosis (FIB-4 >2.67 or NAFLD Fibrosis Score >0.676)
Signs of portal hypertension or cirrhosis
recommended_tests: Liver biopsy if NASH or fibrosis staging needed

diagnoses.name: Alcoholic Liver Disease
key_features: AST:ALT ratio of at least 2:1 (ratio >3:1 further increases likelihood)
AST and ALT rarely exceed 300 IU/L
History of significant alcohol use (>210 g/week men, >140 g/week women)
May present with hepatomegaly, jaundice, or ascites

diagnoses.name: Chronic Hepatitis B
key_features: Often asymptomatic in chronic phase
Risk groups: endemic areas, MSM, injection drug users, dialysis patients, HIV-positive
May present with fatigue, right upper quadrant pain
Fluctuating ALT levels
red_flags: Hepatitis B flare with ALT >10x ULN

diagnoses.name: Chronic Hepatitis C
key_features: Often asymptomatic for decades
Risk groups: IV/intranasal drug use, tattoos, transfusions before 1992, born 1945-1965
Anti-HCV sensitivity 92-97%
Acute HCV typically anicteric and asymptomatic
red_flags: Advanced fibrosis or cirrhosis on presentation

diagnoses.name: Autoimmune Hepatitis
key_features: 4:1 female predominance
Elevated ALT/AST with hypergammaglobulinemia (elevated IgG)
Associated autoimmune conditions (hypothyroidism, ulcerative colitis, Sjogren syndrome, rheumatoid arthritis)
Prevalence approximately 1:6000
red_flags: Acute severe presentation mimicking acute liver failure
Rapid progression to cirrhosis if untreated

diagnoses.name: Drug-Induced Liver Injury (DILI)
key_features: Temporal relationship between drug exposure and liver injury
Can cause hepatocellular, cholestatic, or mixed pattern
Common culprits: acetaminophen, antibiotics, NSAIDs, statins, herbal/dietary supplements
Diagnosis of exclusion after other causes ruled out
red_flags: Hy's Law: hepatocellular injury with jaundice (bilirubin >2x ULN) predicts ~10% mortality
recommended_tests: Timeline of drug exposure vs liver test abnormalities

diagnoses.name: Hereditary Hemochromatosis
key_features: Mildly elevated ALT/AST
Elevated transferrin saturation (>=45%) and/or serum ferritin
Bronze skin pigmentation, diabetes, arthropathy, cardiomyopathy in advanced disease
Most common genetic liver disease in Caucasians
recommended_tests: Iron studies (serum iron, transferrin saturation, ferritin)
HFE gene mutation analysis if transferrin saturation >=45%
Liver biopsy or MRI for iron quantification

diagnoses.name: Wilson Disease
key_features: Patients typically <55 years old
Low serum ceruloplasmin
Kayser-Fleischer rings on slit-lamp examination (pathognomonic)
Neuropsychiatric manifestations may coexist
red_flags: Fulminant hepatic failure (Coombs-negative hemolytic anemia + liver failure)
Acute presentation with very high bilirubin and low alkaline phosphatase
recommended_tests: Liver biopsy with hepatic copper quantification

diagnoses.name: Alpha-1 Antitrypsin Deficiency
key_features: Persistently elevated AST or ALT without other explanation
Coexisting emphysema especially in young non-smoker
PiZZ phenotype associated with liver disease
Can present as neonatal cholestasis or adult cirrhosis

diagnoses.name: Primary Biliary Cholangitis (PBC)
key_features: Cholestatic pattern: elevated alkaline phosphatase with or without elevated bilirubin
Antimitochondrial antibody (AMA) positive in >90% of cases
Fatigue and pruritus as predominant symptoms
Strong female predominance (9:1)
recommended_tests: GGT to confirm hepatic origin of alkaline phosphatase

diagnoses.name: Primary Sclerosing Cholangitis (PSC)
key_features: Cholestatic pattern: elevated alkaline phosphatase
Strong association with inflammatory bowel disease (especially ulcerative colitis)
Multifocal strictures and dilations of bile ducts on cholangiography
Male predominance (2:1)

diagnoses.name: Ischemic Hepatopathy (Shock Liver)
key_features: Massive ALT/AST elevation (often >10,000 IU/L)
Context of hemodynamic instability, cardiac failure, or sepsis
Rapid rise and fall of transaminases
Elevated LDH often disproportionate to ALT

diagnoses.name: Hepatitis A (Acute)
key_features: Acute hepatocellular injury pattern (ALT 5-15x ULN or higher)
Fecal-oral transmission, travel to endemic areas, contaminated food/water
Jaundice, fever, malaise, nausea
Self-limited in most cases
red_flags: Fulminant hepatitis (rare but more common in older adults or chronic liver disease)

also_consider.name: Hepatitis E
also_consider.rationale: Consider in patients returning from endemic areas when hepatitis A, B, and C testing is negative; test with IgM HEV antibody

also_consider.name: Budd-Chiari Syndrome (Hepatic Vein Thrombosis)
also_consider.rationale: Acute right upper quadrant pain with hepatomegaly and ascites; consider in patients with hypercoagulable states or myeloproliferative disorders

also_consider.name: Celiac Disease
also_consider.rationale: Unexplained mild transaminase elevation may be the sole presentation; screen with tissue transglutaminase IgA in persistent unexplained elevation

also_consider.name: Thyroid Disease
also_consider.rationale: Both hyperthyroidism and hypothyroidism can cause abnormal liver chemistries; check TSH in unexplained liver test abnormalities

also_consider.name: Hepatocellular Carcinoma
also_consider.rationale: Consider in patients with cirrhosis or chronic hepatitis B who develop rising AFP, new hepatic mass, or worsening liver function

also_consider.name: Infiltrative Liver Disease (Amyloidosis, Sarcoidosis)
also_consider.rationale: Cholestatic pattern with hepatomegaly; consider in patients with known systemic disease and disproportionately elevated alkaline phosphatase

also_consider.name: Gilbert Syndrome
also_consider.rationale: Isolated unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia with otherwise normal liver tests; affects approximately 5% of the population; benign condition

also_consider.name: Pregnancy-Related Liver Disease (HELLP, Acute Fatty Liver of Pregnancy)
also_consider.rationale: Third trimester liver dysfunction with elevated transaminases; HELLP includes hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, and low platelets -- obstetric emergency

also_consider.name: Congestive Hepatopathy (Cardiac Cirrhosis)
also_consider.rationale: Chronic liver congestion from right heart failure; elevated alkaline phosphatase and bilirubin with hepatomegaly and peripheral edema

also_consider.name: IgG4-Related Cholangitis
also_consider.rationale: Mimics PSC or cholangiocarcinoma but responds to corticosteroids; check IgG4 level when cholestatic pattern with biliary strictures

also_consider.name: Veno-Occlusive Disease (Sinusoidal Obstruction Syndrome)
also_consider.rationale: Hepatomegaly, ascites, and jaundice following hematopoietic stem cell transplant or pyrrolizidine alkaloid exposure

also_consider.name: Glycogenic Hepatopathy
also_consider.rationale: Markedly elevated transaminases in patients with poorly controlled type 1 diabetes; reversible with glycemic control

clinical_reasoning_prompt: This is an evidence-based reference set for evaluating abnormal liver chemistries, not an exhaustive differential. First determine the injury pattern (hepatocellular: ALT/AST predominant; cholestatic: alkaline phosphatase predominant; mixed) and the acuity (acute vs chronic). Always rule out acute liver failure (coagulopathy + encephalopathy) before pursuing a chronic workup. Consider that multiple etiologies may coexist (e.g., NAFLD + alcoholic liver disease, hepatitis C + hemochromatosis). Medication and supplement history is essential in every case. In patients with cirrhosis of any cause, assess severity with Child-Pugh and MELD-Na scores and screen for hepatocellular carcinoma.
